name: Fasting-mimicking diet
lead: The fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) is a five-day, low-calorie, low-protein, plant-based eating cycle designed to reproduce some physiological effects of water fasting while still supplying limited food. It was developed by biogerontologist Valter Longo at the University of Southern California.[1][11]

People use it for a body-composition and skin-and-longevity payoff: a short, structured cycle that cuts calories sharply for five days, which in the 2017 randomized trial was followed by lower body weight, lower body fat and lower blood pressure after three monthly cycles.[2] Proponents describe this as a way to lose fat and shift ageing-related markers without following a restrictive diet every day, and followers in looks-focused spaces discuss it for leaner abdomen, skin and "longevity" aims.[11][13]

Per Grokipedia, a typical cycle supplies roughly 1,000 kcal on day one and about 700 to 800 kcal on days two to five, repeated every one to six months; a commercial version, ProLon, is sold by L-Nutra, founded in 2009.[1] STAT reported in 2017 about 1,100 calories on day one and 800 on each of the next four days, at around $300 per box.[12]

Its main research focus is ageing, metabolic and disease markers rather than appearance. Human data come from a randomized trial of 100 healthy participants and studies in cancer patients; much other work is in mice.[2][3][4]

paras: Unlike intermittent fasting patterns such as time-restricted eating, the FMD is a short periodic cycle rather than a daily or weekly routine. Its nutrient composition is low in calories, sugars and protein and high in unsaturated fats, intended to trigger fasting-like responses.[1][2]

The commercial ProLon box contains pre-packaged soups, crackers, nut bars, olives, herbal teas and supplements sorted by day. A MIT Technology Review writer who completed a cycle described the portions as small and said he lost eight pounds over the five days.[13]

Valter Longo, born in Genoa in 1967, worked in Roy Walford's calorie-restriction lab at UCLA in 1992, earned his PhD at UCLA in 1997 and holds a professorship in gerontology at USC, where he directs the USC Longevity Institute.[11] His group studied fasting and nutrient-sensing pathways from the early 2000s, and the FMD was formalised in the mid-2010s, with a 2015 paper in Cell Metabolism describing a periodic diet that mimics fasting in mice.[1] L-Nutra was founded in 2009 to commercialise the approach.[1]

Longo has said the goal was not weight loss but reducing reliance on pills, which he called prehistoric, and he also recommends time-restricted eating with eating windows of 11 to 12 hours.[11] He wrote The Longevity Diet (2018) and Fasting Cancer (2025), and was named by Time among 50 influential people in health care in 2018.[11]

STAT's 2017 profile reported that L-Nutra sells ProLon and that Longo retained majority ownership, that he said he would direct personal profits to a nonprofit for research, and that about 5,000 people had used the diet, including paying customers and research subjects.[12] After a series of critical articles about ProLon in 2017, Wikipedia says Longo stopped accepting consulting fees and pledged to donate his company shares to charity.[11]

Experts quoted by STAT said more human data were needed. Dietitian Kristen Gradney said it could work but she could not confidently say that it would, and Grant Tinsley raised the open question of whether benefits come from fewer calories or from unique cellular changes; Karmel Allison suggested the mouse results could reflect weight loss rather than a specific effect of fasting.[12] The same article noted that critics found no proof the specific formula works better than other ultra-low-calorie diets or episodic fasting.[12] Longo says the diet should be done under medical supervision and is not appropriate for some people, including those with diabetes.[12] Longo himself told MIT Technology Review that very few people can stick to calorie restriction, which he gave as a reason for the FMD's short format.[13]
In 2012 the BBC documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer featured Longo, and he later appeared in Netflix's The Goop Lab (2020).[11]

A 2017 randomized trial in 100 generally healthy US participants tested repeated FMD cycles against a control diet on markers and risk factors associated with aging, diabetes, cancer and cardiovascular disease.[2] Participants followed the diet for five days a month for three months; the diet group had lower body weight, body fat, blood pressure and IGF-1 afterward, with no serious adverse effects, and control participants later crossed over, giving 71 completers in the analysis, with the authors reporting greater changes in those at higher risk and calling for larger studies.[2]

A 2022 study in cancer patients reported the diet to be safe in that setting, including in 101 patients, and examined effects on metabolism and antitumor immunity; it reported consistent decreases in blood glucose and growth factor concentrations.[3]
The multicentre randomized phase 2 DIRECT trial examined the FMD as an adjunct to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer.[4]
No studies were found measuring effects on facial appearance or skin as primary appearance outcomes.

Mouse studies have examined the FMD in models of multiple sclerosis, cancer immunity, breast cancer with hormone therapy, diabetes with beta-cell regeneration, inflammatory bowel disease and Parkinson disease.[5][6][7][8][9][10]

Grokipedia notes it is not intended as a daily diet and should be undertaken under medical supervision, particularly with eating disorders, pregnancy or certain medical conditions.[1] STAT reported that Longo says it is not appropriate for people with certain conditions such as diabetes.[12] The MIT Technology Review writer described being hungry and grouchy during the cycle.[13]

timeline.event: Longo joins Roy Walford's calorie-restriction lab at UCLA.[11]
L-Nutra founded to commercialise the diet.[1]
Longo and colleagues publish the periodic diet in mice in Cell Metabolism.[1]
Randomized trial in 100 healthy participants published in Science Translational Medicine; STAT profiles Longo and ProLon.[2][12]
MIT Technology Review reporter describes completing a ProLon cycle.[13]
DIRECT trial in breast cancer published.[4]

lore.intro: The FMD is discussed in longevity and fitness circles as a periodic reset that delivers some fasting benefits with a meal kit, and on technical forums such as Hacker News where posts on its research draw long threads.[12][13][14]

claims.claim: A five-day cycle strips body fat quickly
claims.believers: A MIT Technology Review writer who did a cycle reported losing eight pounds over the five days and avoiding junk food afterward.[13]
claims.experts: The 2017 trial reported lower body weight and body fat after three monthly cycles; STAT quoted critics asking whether the effect comes from fewer calories rather than fasting-specific changes.[2][12]

claims.believers: Longo and supporters describe the diet as lowering ageing-related markers such as IGF-1 and blood glucose, building on mouse results.[2][11]
claims.experts: Human data are limited to short trials of risk markers; STAT noted it is unclear whether such effects last or lead to fewer heart attacks or longer lifespan.[2][12]

claims.claim: It improves skin or looks beyond weight
claims.believers: Proponents frame the diet around healthy ageing, and some followers extend that to skin and a youthful appearance.[11]
claims.experts: No published study has measured facial or skin appearance as a primary outcome of the FMD.[2][3][4]

card.summary: A five-day low-calorie cycle from Valter Longo; studied for aging markers and disease, not for looks.
card.note: Human appearance outcomes untested; supervision advised in pregnancy or eating disorders.

quick.overview:
The fasting-mimicking diet is a five-day plant-based, low-calorie, low-protein cycle created by Valter Longo, repeated every few months.

Human trials examine aging and disease markers and cancer-care settings; no study has tested appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It aims to trigger fasting-like responses, such as lower IGF-1 and increased autophagy, without total food abstinence.
quick.risks: Intended as periodic, not daily. Medical supervision is advised with eating disorders, pregnancy or medical conditions.

chain: Five days of about 800 to 1,100 kcal low-protein plant-based meals
Short-term drop in weight, body fat and blood pressure markers
Leaner look and lower ageing-related risk markers, as measured in trials
angle.text: The FMD is used as a monthly cycle by people who want to lose body fat and shift ageing-related markers without eating restrictively every day. In the 2017 trial, participants who completed three cycles had lower body weight and body fat; no study has used facial or skin appearance as the main outcome.
